headline: Can records of European settler deaths explain today's income gaps?
title: The Colonial Origins of Comparative Development: An Empirical Investigation
note: The paper used historical settler mortality as an instrument for present-day institutions. A published comment challenged the assignment and comparability of mortality observations. The original authors disputed the critique. https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.102.6.3059 https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.102.6.3077

headline: Can the last two digits of your Social Security number sway what you bid for wine?
title: “Coherent Arbitrariness”: Stable Demand Curves Without Stable Preferences
note: Participants considered prices derived from their Social Security numbers before stating maximum bids for goods, including wine. The reported association was between the induced anchor and lab valuations.

headline: Does the stock market need a nap after the clocks change?
title: Losing Sleep at the Market: The Daylight Saving Anomaly
note: The authors compared returns after clock-change weekends with returns after ordinary weekends. They reported lower returns after the clocks changed and proposed disrupted sleep as an explanation. An American Economic Review comment challenged the robustness of the clock-change result. The original authors published a reply. https://ideas.repec.org/a/aea/aecrev/v92y2002i4p1251-1256.html https://doi.org/10.1257/00028280260344795

headline: Do shorter winter days scare investors off risk?
title: Winter Blues: A SAD Stock Market Cycle
note: The authors linked the length of daylight to stock returns across markets. They proposed that seasonal affective disorder changes investors’ appetite for risk. Kelly and Meschke reexamined the result and reported no consistent connection between stock returns and the proposed seasonal-depression mechanism. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378426609003240

headline: Will the second-poorest player give money upward to avoid falling into last place?
title: “Last-Place Aversion”: Evidence and Redistributive Implications
note: In a lab allocation game the authors reported patterns consistent with protecting one's rank near the bottom. The lab project's selected contrast did not meet its replication criterion. https://forrt.org/flora-replication-atlas/doi/10.1093/qje/qjt035/

headline: Did companies named “Corona” start trading in sync during the pandemic?
title: Aye Corona! The contagion effects of being named Corona during the COVID-19 pandemic
note: The authors report new correlations among stock returns linked by the word “Corona” during the outbreak. The analysis concerns comovement.

headline: How much trading comes from mixing up companies with similar stock symbols?
title: How much do investors trade because of name/ticker confusion?
note: The authors attribute some turnover comovement among similar names and tickers to mistaken trades. Their model puts the contribution at around 5% of turnover.

headline: Do countries where more people believe in hell grow faster?
title: Religion and Economic Growth across Countries
note: The authors model national growth by religious beliefs and attendance. A reanalysis found the evidence sensitive to the specification and instruments (https://doi.org/10.1002/jae.1245).

headline: Are couples who marry on Valentine’s Day or matching-number dates more likely to divorce?
title: Not your lucky day: Romantically and numerically special wedding date divorce risks
note: Dutch marriage records link distinctive wedding dates to later divorce, with controls for observable couple characteristics.

headline: Does reminding bankers of their jobs make them report more winning coin tosses?
title: Business culture and dishonesty in the banking industry
note: Bank employees answered work-related or general questions before reporting private coin tosses. The analysis inferred dishonesty from aggregate reports. A later study found no significant increase after the same prompt in Middle Eastern or Asia-Pacific banking samples (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1741-y).

headline: Do loan officers approve more loans when the sky is clear?
title: Clouded judgment: The role of sentiment in credit origination
note: The authors use local sunshine as an instrument for sentiment and relate it to approvals and subsequent loan outcomes. Loan officer sentiment is inferred from weather variation.

headline: Does an executive’s zodiac year make corporate investments less efficient?
title: Does the effect of the annual year taboo exist? Empirical evidence from senior managers’ zodiac year and corporate inefficient investment
note: The authors use executives’ zodiac-year timing in models of overinvestment and underinvestment.

headline: Does the wage gap for blonde women change with work experience?
title: Physical appearance and earnings, hair color matters
note: The paper estimates a negative association with wages among less experienced workers and a different pattern among more experienced workers.

headline: Can changing only a stock’s ticker move its price?
title: What's in a Nickname? Price and Volume Effects of a Pure Ticker Symbol Change
note: An event study measured trading around ticker changes that were unaccompanied by changes to corporate names.

headline: Do clever ticker symbols lead to different stock returns?
title: The name game: The importance of resourcefulness, ruses, and recall in stock ticker symbols
venue: The Quarterly Review of Economics and Finance
note: The study groups stock tickers by the kind of wordplay or name cue they use and compares returns.

headline: Do stock returns change when a different Chinese zodiac animal takes over?
title: Zodiac Calendar and Market Returns
note: The paper compares market returns across Chinese zodiac years using historical index data.

headline: Are stock returns different on Friday the 13th across countries?
title: Friday the 13th: International evidence
note: The authors compared returns on Friday the 13th with other trading dates across markets.

headline: Do some types of stocks do better on a particular day of the week?
title: Day of the week and the cross-section of returns
note: The paper separates stock returns by weekday to estimate systematic differences across stock characteristics.

headline: Do share prices react when clocks switch back to winter time?
title: By the light of day: The effect of the switch to winter time on stock markets
venue: Journal of International Financial Markets, Institutions and Money
note: The authors estimate abnormal market returns around switches out of daylight saving time.

headline: Does a manager’s zodiac year change how the company reports earnings?
title: Constraining earnings management through heightened managerial risk perception: Evidence from zodiac-year belief
venue: Journal of Behavioral and Experimental Finance
note: The study treats a manager’s zodiac year as a change in perceived risk and uses accounting proxies for earnings management.

headline: Does a manager’s zodiac year affect the risk in a company’s supply chain?
title: Superstition and Corporate Supply Chain Risk: Evidence From ‘Zodiac Year’ Beliefs in China
note: The authors compare firm-level supply-chain risk measures during executives’ zodiac years and other years.

headline: Are executives less willing to trade company stock in their own zodiac year?
title: Restricting insider trading through increasing managerial risk aversion – A behavioral mechanism
note: The article uses zodiac-year exposure to estimate a relationship between perceived managerial risk and insider trading.

headline: Do baseball umpires make more mistakes when the air is polluted?
title: Air Quality and Error Quantity: Pollution and Performance in a High-Skilled, Quality-Focused Occupation
venue: Journal of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists
note: The study links local pollution measures to discrepancies between called pitches and tracking data.

headline: Does sunshine change how much financial risk people take in an experiment?
title: ’O Sole Mio: An Experimental Analysis of Weather and Risk Attitudes in Financial Decisions
note: The authors relate weather and mood to experimentally elicited risky choices.

headline: Do left-handed people earn less in the long run?
title: The Wages of Sinistrality: Handedness, Brain Structure, and Human Capital Accumulation
note: The paper estimates associations between handedness and later earnings and reports related differences in measured skills.

headline: Do people shift birth dates toward lucky numbers, and does that show up at school?
title: Numerological preferences, timing of births and the long-term effect on schooling
note: The paper uses birth records to examine date preferences and compares later schooling outcomes.

headline: Can counting a CEO’s use of “I” reveal how the company will behave?
title: It's All about Me: Narcissistic Chief Executive Officers and Their Effects on Company Strategy and Performance
note: Indicators include first-person pronouns, prominence in company materials and relative pay. The authors link a combined score to strategy and performance.

headline: Do CEOs with pilot licenses keep different cash balances?
title: Pilot CEOs and Corporate Cash Holdings
note: The study uses a CEO pilot indicator in regressions for corporate cash holdings.

headline: Are firms more socially responsible when their CEOs have daughters?
title: Shaped by their daughters: Executives, female socialization, and corporate social responsibility
note: The study relates executive children’s gender to corporate social responsibility scores.

headline: Are students who study economics more willing to make a corrupt deal in an experiment?
title: Does economics make citizens corrupt?
note: The authors compare students’ behavior in an experimental corruption game by academic background.

headline: Did rough terrain help African regions by making slave raids harder?
title: Ruggedness: The Blessing of Bad Geography in Africa
note: A geographic model relates terrain ruggedness and present income to historical slave exports.

headline: Do better ancestral crop yields predict how patient people are today?
title: The Agricultural Origins of Time Preference
note: The authors link historical agricultural potential to modern survey measures of long-term orientation.

headline: Can a model of prehistoric migration and genetic diversity explain present-day national income?
title: The “Out of Africa” Hypothesis, Human Genetic Diversity, and Comparative Economic Development
note: The paper uses migration distances and estimated diversity in regressions on comparative economic development. A published critique challenges the population-genetics and historical assumptions (https://doi.org/10.1086/669034).

headline: Do local religious beliefs show up in the price of municipal debt?
title: Local religious beliefs and municipal bond market outcomes
note: The study links area-level religious composition to municipal debt market outcomes.

headline: Do Asian stock markets earn extra returns around Lunar New Year?
title: Chinese Lunar New Year effect in Asian stock markets, 1999–2012
venue: The Quarterly Review of Economics and Finance
note: The authors compare market returns around the Lunar New Year across Asian exchanges.

headline: Can shifting the calendar move a January stock premium to Lunar New Year?
title: January effect, Lunar New Year effect, and liquidity preference
note: The study tests calendar-related return patterns and considers liquidity preferences as an explanation.

headline: Do CEOs with shorter or more familiar names get better pay and perks?
title: What’s in a name? Leaders’ names, compensation, and firm performance
note: The paper constructs a name-fluency score and links it to CEO compensation and perks. It reports no corresponding advantage on the measured performance outcomes.

headline: Does an identical product look more expensive in a currency with larger numbers?
title: Effect of Face Value on Product Valuation in Foreign Currencies
note: The researchers varied currency denominations and measured valuation and willingness to pay.

headline: Does a car lose extra value when the odometer rolls over to a new ten-thousand-mile digit?
title: Heuristic Thinking and Limited Attention in the Car Market
note: The authors estimate jumps in used-car auction prices near mileage thresholds.

headline: Will players and test-takers work harder to hit a round number?
title: Round Numbers as Goals: Evidence From Baseball, SAT Takers, and the Lab
note: The authors examine behavior near round milestones in batting averages, SAT scores and laboratory tasks.

headline: Can a regression put a dollar value on more frequent sex?
title: Money, Sex and Happiness: An Empirical Study
note: Using survey data, the authors relate income and sexual frequency to reported happiness and compare the coefficients.

headline: Were modern income differences already taking shape in 1000 BCE?
title: Was the Wealth of Nations Determined in 1000 BC?
note: The researchers build historical technology-adoption measures and relate them to present economic outcomes.

headline: Can potatoes explain a quarter of the Old World’s population and urban growth from 1700 to 1900?
title: The Potato's Contribution to Population and Urbanization: Evidence From a Historical Experiment
note: The authors estimate this share using the timing of introduction and regional differences in suitability for potato cultivation.

headline: Does ancestral exposure to the slave trade explain lower trust today?
title: The Slave Trade and the Origins of Mistrust in Africa
note: The paper matches estimated historical slave exports to modern survey responses about trust.

headline: Did colder weather and slow growth help fuel European witch trials?
title: Witchcraft, Weather and Economic Growth in Renaissance Europe
note: The author relates historical witch-trial data to weather and economic conditions.

headline: Did competition between churches drive where witch trials happened?
title: Witch Trials
note: The paper relates the geography and timing of witch trials to competition between Catholic and Protestant churches.

headline: Did cereal crops help early states form because they were easy to tax?
title: The Origin of the State: Land Productivity or Appropriability?
note: The authors model hierarchy and state emergence against land suitability for cereals compared with other crops.

headline: Can a military IQ test predict who trades stocks well decades later?
title: IQ, trading behavior, and performance
note: The paper links Finnish IQ test scores with trading records and investment outcomes.

headline: Do a CEO’s childhood disasters or exposure to violent crime show up in the firm’s accounts?
title: Financial reporting consequences of CEOs' early-life exposure to disasters and violent crime
note: The paper regresses financial reporting outcomes on indicators of early-life exposures.

headline: Can a CEO’s face predict company profits in one economic climate better than another?
title: The influence of economic context on the relationship between chief executive officer facial appearance and company profits
note: The authors relate trait judgments made from CEO photographs to profitability across economic contexts.

headline: Do baby-faced executives do better in some leadership contexts?
title: The Teddy-Bear Effect: Does Having a Baby Face Benefit Black Chief Executive Officers?
note: The authors compare babyfacedness ratings and business leadership outcomes across photographed executives.

headline: Do companies led by Republican managers borrow or invest less?
title: Corporate Policies of Republican Managers
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
note: The paper estimates policy differences using political contribution records to classify managers.

headline: Are stocks with tickers that spell English words easier to trade?
title: Does Noninformative Text Affect Investor Behavior?
note: The authors classify tickers that spell English words as clever and compare turnover, trading volume and bid–ask spreads.

headline: Do feng shui considerations show up in land and development prices?
title: Feng Shui and Its Impacts on Land and Property Developments
venue: Journal of Urban Planning and Development
note: The authors use a case study and statistical comparisons to connect a feng shui measure to housing prices.

headline: Do people save more when they feel happier?
title: Reversing the question: Does happiness affect consumption and savings behavior?
note: The article uses local weather variation to estimate a link from happiness to household saving and consumption.

headline: Can national stereotypes or historical conflicts explain who trades with whom?
title: Cultural Biases in Economic Exchange?
note: The authors compare bilateral trust measures with proxies for culture and with trade and investment flows.

headline: Does winning an IPO lottery make investors trade more confidently afterward?
title: Does good luck make people overconfident? Evidence from a natural experiment in the stock market
note: The study compares later behavior of winners and losers in random stock allocation and interprets trading changes as overconfidence.

headline: Do companies borrow or invest differently depending on the religion of the surrounding community?
title: Does religion matter in corporate decision making in America?
note: The paper uses regional religious composition to model differences in corporate risk-taking and financial policies.

headline: Does local religiosity predict how firms report their finances?
title: Religious Social Norms and Corporate Financial Reporting
note: The study relates county-level religious adherence to indicators of financial reporting decisions.

headline: Can the boss’s zodiac year change the measured risk of the company?
title: Management’s superstition and company risk: Evidence from the Chinese zodiac year belief
note: The researchers use executive zodiac years as a proxy for superstition in firm-risk regressions.

headline: Did moving-average trading rules work beyond the stock history used to find them?
title: Simple Technical Trading Rules and the Stochastic Properties of Stock Returns
note: The original analysis tested technical rules on historical Dow data. A later analysis examined a larger search universe with a data-snooping adjustment and tested the rules on later observations. https://doi.org/10.1111/0022-1082.00163

headline: Does expecting more pay make you work longer even when the pay rule is unchanged?
title: Reference Points and Effort Provision
note: Participants could stop a real-effort task and receive either task earnings or a fixed payment determined by chance. The original reported more work under a higher fixed-payment possibility. A later replication did not recover the focal effect under its criterion. https://forrt.org/flora-replication-atlas/doi/10.1257/aer.101.2.470/

headline: Did charging late parents make more of them show up late?
title: A Fine is a Price
note: In an Israeli daycare field experiment, late pickups increased after a small fine was introduced. A follow-up in a tax experiment examined how contingent the outcome was on the design. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.irle.2020.105906

headline: Do stocks with easier-to-pronounce names rise faster after listing?
title: Predicting short-term stock fluctuations by using processing fluency
note: The paper combined an experiment on judgments with analyses of newly listed stocks and ticker pronounceability. The reported relationship varied by time horizon. A later study used a different name-fluency measure. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304405X13001141

headline: Can paying a tiny amount make people do worse than paying them nothing?
title: Pay Enough or Don't Pay at All
note: In the reported tasks, including a test and a donation-collection exercise, low incentives could produce lower performance than no personal pay. Higher pay outperformed lower pay within paid conditions.

headline: Do CEOs get a raise when oil prices rise even though they did not set the price?
title: Are CEOs Rewarded for Luck? The Ones Without Principals Are
note: The authors isolated company-performance fluctuations tied to external factors and related them to chief executive pay. Estimated pay for favorable shocks varied with measures of corporate governance.

headline: Does a sunny morning give the stock market a lift?
title: Good Day Sunshine: Stock Returns and the Weather
note: The authors matched morning weather in the cities hosting 26 countries’ main stock exchanges with daily index returns. Sunnier mornings were associated with higher returns.

headline: The national team lost. Is the stock market next?
title: Sports Sentiment and Stock Returns
note: The authors compared international sports results with national stock indices. After a country lost a World Cup knockout match, the average next-day return was 0.49 percentage points below the benchmark.

headline: Do companies file more innovative patents when the CEO flies planes for fun?
title: Pilot CEOs and corporate innovation
note: The authors used pilot credentials as a measure of sensation seeking and compared firms on patent counts, citations, and novelty measures. They interpreted the patent differences as evidence about a CEO personality trait, using a hobby as its proxy.

headline: Can speeding tickets predict how often someone trades stocks?
title: Sensation Seeking, Overconfidence, and Trading Activity
note: The authors linked Finnish driving records, psychological profiles, and equity trades. They treated speeding tickets as a proxy for sensation seeking and used trading frequency to examine whether that trait carries over to investment behavior.

headline: Can a county's Catholic-to-Protestant ratio predict which companies will innovate?
title: Local Gambling Preferences and Corporate Innovative Success
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
note: The researchers used the ratio of Catholics to Protestants in a firm's headquarters county as a proxy for local gambling preferences. They related that county-level proxy to R&D, patent outcomes, and project risk, and proposed a link between local attitudes toward gambling and corporate innovation.

headline: Can disasters near a CEO's childhood home predict how much risk the company takes?
title: What Doesn't Kill You Will Only Make You More Risk-Loving: Early-Life Disasters and CEO Behavior
note: The authors linked CEOs' early-life locations to records of fatal disasters. Their estimates pointed to more corporate risk-taking at intermediate levels of exposure and less at extreme levels. They interpreted the fitted pattern as evidence about how early-life experiences shape later risk preferences.

headline: Can a CEO's home mortgage predict how much debt the company takes on?
title: Behavioral consistency in corporate finance: CEO personal and corporate leverage
note: The authors related leverage on CEOs' primary homes to corporate leverage, along with tests around CEO turnover. They interpreted the relationship as evidence of a consistent approach to borrowing across personal and corporate decisions.

headline: Do stocks get traded more just because their company names come earlier in the alphabet?
title: Alphabetic Bias, Investor Recognition, and Trading Behavior
note: The study estimated 5–15% higher trading activity and liquidity for U.S. stocks near the top of alphabetical listings than for those near the bottom. The authors proposed investor recognition as the explanation for the relationship.

headline: Can a photo rating predict whether someone owns stocks?
title: Beauty and stock market participation
note: The study linked photo-based attractiveness ratings from the Wisconsin Longitudinal Survey to respondents' stock ownership and the share of wealth invested in stocks. The authors examined several possible explanations for the relationship between appearance and investment.

headline: Does Wall Street trade less on Yom Kippur and rally before St. Patrick's Day?
title: Nonsecular Regularities in Returns and Volume
note: The study compared U.S. market returns and volume around religious and cultural occasions. The authors discussed festive or solemn moods as explanations for some return patterns, including lower returns after Yom Kippur in the second half of the sample.

headline: Do CEOs make more deals when they get married or divorced?
title: “I Do”: Does Marital Status Affect How Much CEOs “Do”?
note: The study linked changes in CEOs' marital status to company deal-making and firm risk. The authors explored whether marriage and divorce could reveal unobserved risk preferences that carry over to corporate decisions.

headline: Can changing a fund's name to match the latest investing fad attract money?
title: Changing Names with Style: Mutual Fund Name Changes and Their Effects on Fund Flows
note: The authors estimated an average 28% cumulative abnormal inflow in the year after a fund adopted a name associated with a popular style. They reported no improvement in performance and examined whether the name change itself attracted attention.

headline: Do markets react more strongly to news just because a stock has a lower price per share?
title: Can the Market Multiply and Divide? Non-Proportional Thinking in Financial Markets
note: The study compared percentage-return volatility and responses to news across nominal share prices and around stock splits. The authors interpreted larger percentage moves at lower nominal prices as evidence that investors think in dollars per share.

headline: How much value does Santa destroy each Christmas?
title: The Deadweight Loss of Christmas
note: Students estimated what their Christmas gifts had cost and what those gifts were worth to them. The author used the gap to estimate how much value was lost through gift giving.

headline: Sell in May and sit out the market until Halloween?
title: The Halloween Indicator, “Sell in May and Go Away”: Another Puzzle
note: The authors split the trading year in two. In 36 of the 37 markets they examined, average returns from November through April exceeded those from May through October.

headline: Want to hire a profitable trader? Measure his fingers?
title: Second-to-fourth digit ratio predicts success among high-frequency financial traders
note: The researchers measured the fingers of 44 male traders in London. Within that group, traders whose index fingers were shorter relative to their ring fingers had higher long-term trading profits.

headline: Can the Super Bowl winner predict whether the stock market rises?
title: An Examination of the Super Bowl Stock Market Predictor
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Want tenure in economics? An A surname might help.
title: What's in a Surname? The Effects of Surname Initials on Academic Success
note: At the top ten US economics departments, tenured faculty were more likely to have surnames near the start of the alphabet. The authors pointed to the discipline’s practice of listing coauthors alphabetically.

headline: Can Twitter's mood predict the Dow Jones?
title: Twitter mood predicts the stock market
note: The authors extracted mood scores from Twitter posts and reported improved forecasting performance for the Dow Jones Industrial Average in their dataset.

headline: Can a trader’s morning spit predict his day’s profits?
title: Endogenous steroids and financial risk taking on a London trading floor
note: Researchers collected saliva from male traders on a London trading floor. On days when a trader had higher morning testosterone, he also tended to earn more.

headline: Can the shape of a CEO's face predict company performance?
title: A Face Only an Investor Could Love: CEOs’ Facial Structure Predicts Their Firms’ Financial Performance
note: The paper relates CEOs' facial proportions to company financial performance.

headline: How much is the company worth? Check the CEO’s golf calendar.
title: FORE! An Analysis of CEO Shirking
note: The authors used rounds of golf as a measure of CEO leisure. The most frequent golfers ran firms with lower operating performance and lower valuations.

headline: Meant to buy MCIC. Bought MCI instead?
title: Massively Confused Investors Making Conspicuously Ignorant Choices (MCI–MCIC)
note: The author compared two securities with similar ticker symbols. Their short-term returns, trading volume and volatility moved together, a pattern he attributed to investors mixing them up.

headline: What was a dot-com name worth during the internet boom?
title: A Rose.com by Any Other Name
note: The authors tracked firms that announced a switch to an internet-related name. Over the ten days surrounding the announcement, their shares gained about 74% more than the benchmark.

headline: Do CEOs with deeper voices run bigger companies?
title: Voice pitch and the labor market success of male chief executive officers
note: The authors relate male CEO voice pitch to firm size and compensation.

headline: Is a lucky stock code bad luck for investors?
title: Superstition and Financial Decision Making
note: Among newly listed Chinese companies, the authors found more lucky numerical stock codes than chance would predict. Stocks with those codes had lower benchmark-adjusted returns after listing.

headline: Should US investors avoid the World Cup?
title: Exploitable Predictable Irrationality: The FIFA World Cup Effect on the U.S. Stock Market
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
note: The authors reported lower US market returns during World Cup effect periods than comparison periods and proposed a trading strategy.

headline: Does Mercury retrograde knock 3.47% off annualized stock returns?
title: Cultural beliefs and equity prices: Evidence from astrological belief in mercury retrograde
note: The authors reported a lower annualized market return during retrograde periods across 48 countries and interpreted it through investor beliefs.

headline: Should investors check the moon before buying stocks?
title: Are investors moonstruck? Lunar phases and stock returns
note: The authors grouped stock returns from 48 countries by the phase of the moon. Average returns were lower around a full moon than around a new moon.

headline: Can the mood of music listeners predict next week's stock returns?
title: Music sentiment and stock returns around the world
note: Researchers used the mood of music streamed by listeners as a sentiment indicator. They reported positive contemporaneous return associations and negative next-week associations.

headline: Does reminding people of their religion change how much they chip in?
title: Religious Identity and Economic Behavior
note: Researchers experimentally made religious identity salient. They reported contrasting effects on public-good contributions by religious affiliation. These estimates come from a laboratory contribution task.

headline: Do economics students cooperate less after studying economics?
title: Does Studying Economics Inhibit Cooperation?
note: The authors compared students' responses and behavior across tasks and discussed both education and selection. A published response challenged the generalization and examined other measures of cooperation. https://doi.org/10.1257/jep.10.1.177

headline: Can framing the same poetry reading turn someone's desired fee into a bid to attend?
title: Tom Sawyer and the Construction of Value
note: Participants first contemplated either paying for or being paid to hear a poetry reading. Initial framing changed how they subsequently valued the experience.

headline: Did stock returns jump just before market holidays?
title: High Stock Returns before Holidays: Existence and Evidence on Possible Causes
note: This historical study found higher mean returns before market holidays. Later out-of-sample research reported that the premium was largely concentrated in small firms. https://www.emerald.com/cfr/article-abstract/13/3-4/531/1326451/The-Pre-Holiday-Premium-of-Ariel-1990-Has-Largely

headline: Can Google searches for a ticker forecast a short-lived price rise?
title: In Search of Attention
note: The study used search volume as an investor-attention proxy and related spikes to short-run price increases and subsequent reversal. Search volume and returns were measured from observed data.

headline: Can the tone of a newspaper column predict tomorrow's market moves?
title: Giving Content to Investor Sentiment: The Role of Media in the Stock Market
note: The analysis measured pessimistic language in a Wall Street Journal column and found associations with near-term price pressure and subsequent reversal. Text tone was a measured proxy for sentiment.

headline: Can a county's religious composition predict demand for lottery-like stocks?
title: Religious Beliefs, Gambling Attitudes, and Financial Market Outcomes
note: The study used local religious composition as a proxy for attitudes toward gambling and related it to financial outcomes. Area-level composition and personal beliefs are distinct measurements.

headline: Can the price of a closed-end fund measure investors' mood?
title: Investor Sentiment and the Closed-End Fund Puzzle
note: The authors interpreted common movement in closed-end fund discounts using an investor-sentiment account and tested predictions relating discounts to other outcomes.

headline: Can a bubble form when traders cannot buy a share and sell it on to someone else?
title: Nonspeculative Bubbles in Experimental Asset Markets: Lack of Common Knowledge of Rationality vs. Actual Irrationality
note: The researchers still observed prices departing from the benchmark in a laboratory design that ruled out resale speculation for individual traders.

headline: Can January's stock market predict the Super Bowl winner?
title: Exploring a market curiosity: an examination of the Super Bowl Indicator
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Can storms on the Sun predict stock returns on Earth?
title: Playing the field: Geomagnetic storms and international stock markets
venue: Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta Working Paper 2003-5
note: The working paper reported that unusually high geomagnetic activity in the preceding week predicted lower stock returns in several markets.

headline: Do Chinese investors earn less in their own zodiac year?
title: Impact of perceived unlucky years on investment performance: Evidence from Chinese cultural beliefs
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Can the size of a CEO's signature reveal bad investments?
title: Narcissism is a bad sign: CEO signature size, investment, and performance
note: CEO signature size is used as a narcissism proxy in a study of investment and financial results.

headline: Born in June or July? What are your odds of becoming CEO?
title: The relative-age effect and career success: Evidence from corporate CEOs
note: June and July birthdays were underrepresented among the CEOs in the sample. The authors suggested that children born in those months might have been among the youngest in their class.

headline: Do unlucky dates produce better stock returns in Asian markets?
title: Superstitions and stock trading: some new evidence
venue: Journal of the Asia Pacific Economy
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Would you buy a stock called MOO?
title: Would a stock by any other ticker smell as sweet?
venue: The Quarterly Review of Economics and Finance
note: The authors picked out memorable ticker symbols, including MOO and LUV. From 1984 to 2005, the stocks in that group earned higher average daily returns than the market as a whole.

headline: Can a CEO's face tell investors how risky a firm is?
title: The face of risk: CEO facial masculinity and firm risk
note: The paper links CEO facial width-to-height ratios to firm risk measures.

headline: Can a CEO's facial proportions predict tax avoidance?
title: Do more masculine-faced CEOs reflect more tax avoidance? Evidence from Indonesia
note: The researchers measure facial ratios and relate them to corporate tax avoidance measures.

headline: Do lucky digits in Taiwanese ticker codes earn higher returns?
title: Lucky issuance: The role of numerological superstitions in irrational return premiums
note: The authors compared returns of Taiwanese listed firms grouped by digits considered lucky or unlucky in their stock codes.

headline: Do stock markets make fast profits during Ramadan?
title: Fast profits: Investor sentiment and stock returns during Ramadan
note: Daily equity returns in 14 predominantly Muslim countries were compared across calendar periods; the paper reported higher returns during Ramadan.

headline: Can an aviation disaster move the entire stock market?
